cards.title: Audit as constraint diagnosis, not settings checklist
cards.summary: Structure an ad-account audit as a ranked diagnosis of the single business constraint, delivered as a prioritized 90-day roadmap.
cards.use_when: You are planning a quarterly audit of your paid media account or deciding whether an incoming audit document is worth acting on.
steps: Reject audits that are just 40+ screenshots of settings errors with generic recommendations; the source calls these a '1-enter at best' because most settings debates are subjective and rarely contextualized to the business.
Instead, treat the audit as a diagnosis of the constraint: identify the one bottleneck holding back growth, prove it with data, and give clear next steps ordered by commercial impact.
Organize the diagnosis across three pillars: (1) technical account structure, (2) creative velocity and diversity, (3) data integrity and assurance.
Rank every recommendation by commercial impact so the output reads as a sequenced roadmap you can execute over roughly 90 days, not a flat list.
Deliver the audit as a narrated screen-share walkthrough (the source uses Loom) showing the actual account, the model, and the fix, so the team can distribute and act on it.
Re-derive the pillar framework for your own business rather than copying the source's—the source states these pillars are their current thesis and will evolve.
caveats: The three-pillar framework is presented as the source's opinion, not a universal standard.
Source context: agency managing $400M+/year in ad spend across 60 eight- and nine-figure brands, ~1,000 audits over six years.

cards.title: Refuse to audit without business-level KPI access
cards.summary: An ad audit is only valid if you can see business KPIs (cost per new customer, gross profit), not just platform-reported ROAS.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether you can run a meaningful audit with the data you currently have access to, or selecting an agency that only reports platform metrics.
steps: Pull backend numbers from your commerce system (e.g., Shopify or other CMS) rather than starting inside Meta or Google.

If you only have Facebook and Google platform data, stop and get backend access first — the source refuses to proceed with audits constrained to platform data because the entire data-integrity pillar becomes impossible.
Compute cost to acquire a customer from the business side: total advertising spend divided by new customers per month.
Pair it with gross profit on first purchase in dollars, because unit economics move over time — a $100 AOV at 60% GP is not comparable to a $200 AOV at 80% GP.
Do not accept platform-attributed ROAS as a substitute for business-level acquisition metrics.
caveats: Source's stated policy: they will not audit or pitch on platform data alone — this is their standard for scaling work, not a general industry rule.

cards.title: Build a 2–2.5 year CAC and GP-per-customer cohort model
cards.summary: Graph monthly CAC, gross profit on first purchase, and new-customer volume over 2–2.5 years to see whether efficiency is trending right or wrong.
cards.use_when: You need a top-level read on whether your paid acquisition economics are improving or deteriorating before drilling into platforms.
steps: Build columns in a spreadsheet: month, CAC (total ad spend / new customers), gross profit on first purchase in dollars, and GP-to-CAC ratio (GP cell divided by CAC cell) for each month, ideally going back 2–2.5 years.

Derive GP per first order either by multiplying historical average order value by gross margin % from the P&L (accrual accounting), or by pulling average gross margin on first order from your commerce system if cost of goods is tagged historically.
Avoid plugging a flat GP assumption — the source stresses data integrity here.
Add a new-customer volume column, then graph volume, CAC, and GP over time.

Read the trend: if CAC is rising but new-customer volume is flat or barely up, spend has risen without buying more customers — a problem. If CAC rose while volume tripled or quadrupled, the trade-off can be worth it.
Use the trend to decide whether to scale, hold and optimize, or pull back — the source warns that forcing unprofitable cohorts puts you in a bad position 3–6 months later.
caveats: This GP-to-CAC figure is first-purchase only, so the source notes it is not technically lifetime gross profit.
No universal benchmark is established; the ratio bands are source heuristics.

cards.title: GP-to-CAC ratio bands for scale, hold, or pull back
cards.summary: Use first-purchase gross profit divided by CAC to judge whether current economics justify scaling spend.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to increase ad budgets, hold flat, or cut spend based on first-order profitability.
steps: Calculate the ratio as first-purchase gross profit in dollars divided by CAC for the current month and over time.

Interpret per the source's bands: under 1 means you lose money on the first purchase (high bankruptcy risk unless you are a well-capitalized CPG with strong retention); 1–2 is 'fine' but generally not scale-worthy without strong retention; 2–3 is the target zone where the source says scale; above 3 means you are likely leaving money on the table.

Adjust these bands for retention: strong repeat purchase behavior supports a higher CAC tolerance and a lower first-purchase ratio, and weak retention requires being very profitable on first purchase because people do not buy again.
Check the trend line, not just the current month: deteriorating ratio over the last 6 months is the signal to investigate before scaling.
caveats: Bands are source-specific heuristics, not calculated benchmarks.
The source notes these bands assume no other acquisition channel is excluded from the calculation.
Figure is first-purchase only, not true lifetime gross profit.

cards.title: Normalized P&L for volume verification
cards.summary: Build a 2–2.5 year normalized P&L to check whether contribution margin improves or degrades as you ramp ad spend.
cards.use_when: You are verifying whether scaling ad spend produced profitable volume or just bought top-line revenue.
steps: Structure the P&L: gross revenue minus refunds/returns minus discounts plus shipping collected equals net revenue; then subtract cost of goods sold, shipping and fulfillment, and transaction fees to reach gross margin; then subtract marketing (all channels in one line); this yields contribution profit/margin.
Enter monthly data for the last 2–2.5 years.

If you are an in-house brand, you may continue down through operating expenses to EBITDA; if you are an agency doing a client audit, stop before operating expenses — the source says they are not needed.
Track the contribution margin trend: if margin is falling while you are ramping ad spend, that scaling attempt failed.
Identify at what spend level the failure happened and what assumptions about generating more revenue at higher spend proved wrong.
Use this to confirm or contradict the unit-level CAC read from the cohort model.
caveats: Refunds, discounts, shipping collected, and fee structures vary by commerce system and accounting method.
The source describes this as a verification step, not the primary metric.

cards.title: First-time-customer P&L to expose weak acquisition
cards.summary: Filter out returning-customer revenue to see true new-customer acquisition performance and compute acquisition MER.
cards.use_when: Your blended P&L looks healthy but you suspect paid acquisition is actually underperforming.
steps: Regenerate the P&L filtering out all returning-customer orders, keeping only first-time orders.
Compare it to the blended P&L: the source notes that accumulated repeat revenue can make an eight- or nine-figure retailer's acquisition look far better than it is.
Compute acquisition MER from this filtered P&L: new customer revenue divided by ad spend.
Use this acquisition MER as the reference point for the data-integrity comparison against platform ROAS.

The source's illustrative range: large retailers often see acquisition MER of roughly 3x to 7x — for every $1 of ad spend, $3–$7 of new customer revenue; a $100k monthly spend would mean $300k–$700k in new customer sales.
caveats: The 3x–7x figure is an illustrative example from the source, not a benchmark.
Filtering methods depend on how your commerce system tags first-time versus repeat orders.

cards.title: Reconcile platform ROAS with acquisition MER
cards.summary: Detect over-attribution by comparing platform account-wide ROAS against the acquisition MER from your first-time P&L.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to trust Meta, Google, TikTok, or Pinterest reported ROAS for budget decisions.
steps: Pull the account-wide ROAS from each platform and place it next to the acquisition MER from the first-time P&L.

If the gap is large (the source's example: P&L says $3–$7 back per dollar, Meta account-wide says 17), suspect one-day-view attribution crediting conversions to people who would have bought anyway, or overspend on existing customers inflating the number.
On Meta, click columns, run an attribution-setting breakdown, and inspect 7-day click and 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view, plus incremental attribution.
The source says in ~95% of accounts these tighter settings correlate much better with acquisition MER.
Choose one: switch all attribution settings to the tightest-correlating option, or keep current settings but judge performance using the breakdown numbers rather than the headline ROAS.

On TikTok and Pinterest, pull 7-day-click ROAS; the source says one-day view typically inflates TikTok substantially and 7-day click will drop toward (or below) acquisition MER. Repeat the correlation exercise for every platform.
caveats: The 17x versus 3–7x and the ~95% figure are source illustrations/assertions, not measured guarantees.
Attribution interface labels and available breakdowns change; verify the current platform UI before acting.

cards.title: Google: check brand/non-brand split and non-brand correlation
cards.summary: Keep brand and non-brand campaigns cleanly separated and test non-brand ROAS against acquisition MER.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating whether Google Search/Shopping is genuinely acquiring new customers or harvesting existing demand.
steps: Do not tighten Google's wide default attribution windows — the source says Google is data-reliant and recommends leaving long windows in place rather than narrowing them.
Instead, check for clear separation between branded and non-branded campaigns; brand keywords appearing in non-brand campaigns (or vice versa) is an immediate red flag to fix.

Look at your non-branded campaigns' ROAS against acquisition MER. If they do not correlate, investigate three possibilities: (a) they are genuinely outperforming and you may be underspending on Google, (b) they are mislabeled — pulling brand or bottom-of-funnel traffic driven from other channels, or (c) there is a setup/attribution problem.
Only after ruling out (a) and (b) should you conclude it is a setup issue.
caveats: Google's attribution defaults and reports change; verify current settings in the interface.
Bottom-of-funnel and cross-channel halo effects make Google ROAS misreadings common in the source's experience.

cards.title: Isolate a test to resolve attribution ambiguity
cards.summary: When correlation between platform ROAS and business MER stays unresolved, run a controlled incrementality test instead of guessing.
cards.use_when: You cannot tell whether a platform (Meta, Google, TikTok) is genuinely driving incremental new-customer revenue.
steps: Once you have compared platform ROAS to acquisition MER and attribution-setting changes still do not reconcile them, do not keep spending on an assumption — design a test.
For eight- and nine-figure brands, the source uses causal geo-lift experiments, typically run over about 25 days, to validate a platform's incrementality.
For brand-spend incrementality, use a clustering algorithm to pull brand spend from selected states and measure the effect, if the business believes brand is incremental.
Write clear parameters before launching so the result is readable; the output should either confirm performance or confirm a setup problem.
caveats: ~25 days is the source's typical duration, not a fixed rule.
Geo tests require sufficient volume; the source frames this as an eight/nine-figure technique.

cards.title: Evaluate retention to set CAC targets
cards.summary: Benchmark gross-profit retention curves by day 90, 180, and 365 to decide how much first-purchase CAC you can tolerate.
cards.use_when: You are setting acquisition budget targets and need to know whether high first-order CAC is justified by repeat purchasing.
steps: Build a cohort analysis at gross profit level over time.
Examine the percentage growth in gross profit at day 90, day 180, and day 365.
Compare your curve against portfolio averages for comparable brands/categories — the source contrasts e.g. fashion brands against each other.

Use the result to adjust CAC tolerance: strong retention means a higher acceptable CAC and lower first-purchase GP-to-CAC requirement; poor retention means first purchase must be highly profitable because people do not buy again.
Feed the adjusted tolerance back into your new-customer KPI targets.
caveats: Pulling these numbers is described as complicated; the source does not give universal growth benchmarks in this video.
Comparisons are to the source's client-portfolio averages, which are category-dependent.

cards.title: One cold campaign until business complexity forces a split
cards.summary: Start account structure from a single cold campaign and require a defendable purpose for every additional campaign.
cards.use_when: You are restructuring a Meta or Google ad account or reviewing whether campaign count is inflated.
steps: Ask: how many campaigns exist, and what is the defendable purpose of each one? Write each purpose into a spreadsheet column next to the campaign.
Error-check each campaign against its stated purpose (exclusions, settings, creative) as you go.

Cut any campaign you cannot defend with a clear commercial argument and consolidate; the source says this is common even in accounts spending $1M–$5M/month, and consolidation usually improves performance.
Do not add complexity for spend's sake — the source says complexity is required by business complexity, not budget size.

Legitimate causes of fragmentation include multiple countries/sub-brands/regions where you want to shift budget selectively (e.g., Australia vs New Zealand), or a fast-turning product portfolio where you need to pull budget on one category (e.g., dresses) and read results quickly.
If your agency cannot articulate why each campaign exists, treat that as a reason to consolidate.
caveats: This is the source's operating thesis for their managed accounts, not an industry rule.
Meta 'campaign count' heuristics change with platform behavior; validate against current performance.

cards.title: Check frequency across new, engaged, and existing audiences
cards.summary: Use 30-day frequency on new/engaged/existing segments to find overspend and weak top-of-funnel content.
cards.use_when: You are diagnosing audience-segment budget distribution or diagnosing creative fatigue in your Meta account.
steps: Split budget analysis by three segments: new, engaged, and existing — the source says look at frequency, not percentage split, across these.
If 30-day frequency on existing is extreme (source example: 30), you are overspending on existing customers and should cut that spend.
If frequency on engaged is high (source example: 14), you have too much middle-of-funnel creative and should reduce it in favor of more top-of-funnel assets.
Treat high engaged frequency as a symptom of content that is not top-of-funnel enough, or of existing-customer spend bleeding into all campaigns instead of being controlled in a dedicated campaign.
Fix by launching more genuinely top-of-funnel assets and containing existing-customer spend to one dedicated campaign.
caveats: The 30 and 14 figures are illustrative source examples, not universal thresholds.
Ideal frequency varies by category and offer; do not treat a single frequency number as a target without context.

cards.title: Standardize on 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view
cards.summary: Adopt a single tight attribution setting across the account and keep it consistent.
cards.use_when: You are configuring Meta attribution settings or auditing whether settings are inconsistent across campaigns.
steps: Check whether attribution settings are consistent across all campaigns; inconsistency changes reported ROAS between campaigns and muddies comparisons.
Choose a tighter setting that correlates better with your P&L; the source's go-to is 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view.

Note the source's explanation for including engaged views: Meta changed the definition roughly three months before the video so that likes/comments/shares and 5-second views are no longer counted in 7-day click, so 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view is roughly equivalent to the previously preferred 7-day click.
Apply the same attribution setting everywhere, then use attribution-setting breakdowns when judging performance (see reconcile-platform-roas card).
caveats: The specific definition change and closure equivalence is time-sensitive; verify current Meta documentation.
A 'tighter' setting is a business-fit choice, not universally optimal — the source notes it correlates better with their P&L.

cards.title: Audit campaign naming against actual settings and creative
cards.summary: Confirm that campaign/adset naming matches the targeting, objective, and creative actually running underneath.
cards.use_when: You are doing a housekeeping pass or suspect high-ROAS 'cold' campaigns are mislabeled warm or existing-customer campaigns.
steps: For each campaign/adset, compare the name to the actual audience definition, placement, objective, and the ads beneath it.

Flag mismatches: source notes a campaign labeled 'cold top of funnel' frequently turns out to target existing customers and serve bottom-of-funnel assets, making its ROAS look great when it is not actually acquiring cold customers.

If names use awareness stages (e.g., 'problem aware'), verify the ads actually match that stage (a 'problem aware' adset running a bunch of solution-aware ads is a defect even if the name looks competent).
Treat naming mismatch as a diagnosis gap: the account is claiming something the traffic and creative are not delivering.
caveats: Naming conventions vary; the criterion is whether the label accurately describes the audience and creative, not a specific label format.

cards.title: Common Meta settings errors worth fixing
cards.summary: A short list of concrete Meta account errors: undefined segments, App Rewards placements, legacy lookalike/interest targeting on purchase objectives, missing existing-customer exclusions.
cards.use_when: You are doing a settings-and-targeting error sweep on a Meta account during a structure audit.
steps: Set definitions on new, engaged, and existing audiences rather than leaving them undefined.
Kill App Rewards placements — the source says they have never seen an App Rewards placement drive a single purchase, and local/store-driving engaged-view campaigns bleed into this placement.

Do not use legacy targeting methods (lookalikes, interest targeting) on purchase objectives for ecommerce; the source would not use them for 99% of accounts, reserving them for specific non-purchase cases.
Verify existing customers are actually excluded from cold campaigns.
Confirm naming matches settings and creative (see separate card).
caveats: '99% of accounts' and the no-purchases-from-App-Rewards claim are the source's stated opinions/experience, not measured benchmarks.
Placement options and defaults change over time; verify in the current ads manager.

cards.title: Google-specific audit checks: search terms, feed, currency
cards.summary: Audit Google by checking brand leakage in cold campaigns, Merchant Center feed completeness, and multi-currency feed setup.
cards.use_when: You are auditing Google Ads and Google Merchant Center ahead of a seasonal peak or a restructure.
steps: Open each cold campaign, go to search terms, and verify branded terms are not pulling through into cold campaigns.
Check the Google Merchant Center feed: optimize titles, fill in all relevant feed variables, and eliminate warnings and errors.

If selling across multiple countries, use a multi-currency feed — the source warns that running everything through a single currency triggers auto-conversion and adds tax as it presents in Shopping, hurting performance.
Then investigate the halo effect: Google often sits bottom-of-funnel, so check whether cold search-term demand is genuinely converting cold traffic.

If ROAS on non-brand campaigns does not correlate with acquisition MER after these checks, the source usually proposes an incrementality test for Google — but only when they suspect a halo effect or need rigorous validation.
caveats: The source notes Google can be a strong new-customer channel — one of their own brands was Google-only and reached a seven-figure run rate around 2019–2020 — so Google is not inherently bottom-of-funnel.
Feed and interface details change; verify current GMC and Google Ads UI.

cards.title: Creative volume rule: one new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend
cards.summary: Size your creative production requirement by anchoring new ads per month to monthly ad spend.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether creative volume is the bottleneck or setting a production target for your creative team or agency.
steps: Divide monthly ad spend by $1,000 to get a baseline monthly new-ad target (source example: $100k/month implies ~100 new ads per month).
Treat this as a rough rule of thumb, not a linear law — the source says at $1–3M/month you likely do not need 3,000 assets, and there are diminishing returns to raw creative volume at large scale.

If you need a more precise target, use one of two models: (a) a churn model — monthly churn rate of winners implies a replacement rate; combine with hit rate to back into volume; or (b) average winner spend and revenue generation — if an average winner generates $20k, use that and your win rate to back-propagate to volume.
If your actual output is far below the rule-of-thumb target, treat creative volume as a likely bottleneck.
caveats: $1,000/ad is explicitly a simplification; the source's real models are described as complicated.
Churn-model inputs (winner churn, hit rate, average winner revenue) are business-specific and must come from your own account.

cards.title: Separate volume, diversity, and quality as the creative bottleneck
cards.summary: Creative bottlenecks are one of exactly three: insufficient volume, insufficient concept diversity, or insufficient quality.
cards.use_when: You are diagnosing why creative performance has plateaued and need to pick the right fix.
steps: First check volume against your spend-based target (see the $1,000/new-ad card); if output is far off, that is the bottleneck.
If volume is fine, check diversity — specifically concept diversification, not format diversification (see concept-diversity card).

If both volume and diversity are adequate, assess quality by reading the actual scripts and content, judging angles, personas, scripting, talent, and offer. This is the hardest to systematize and requires direct-response marketing judgment; the source recommends looking at the ads directly and rescripting/reshooting what is weak.
Assign exactly one bottleneck at a time — the source emphasizes you only have one creative bottleneck at any moment; pick it and fix it before moving on.
caveats: Quality has no SOP in the source — it requires domain judgment and reviewing actual creative.
You may end up with a different bottleneck than the source would call it if your spend model differs.

cards.title: Diversify concepts, not just formats
cards.summary: Measure creative diversity by angle/offer/persona concept coverage rather than by mix of UGC, statics, and other formats.
cards.use_when: You are planning creative strategy for a scaling account or diagnosing why a single winning ad fatigues.
steps: Define concepts as a combination of angle, offer, and persona — not format (video vs static vs UGC). The source says people over-index on format diversity and under-index on concept diversity.

Illustration: a creatine brand spending $200k/month may be launching 200 ads/month but if all spend sits behind one concept (e.g., men 25–45, gym-performance angle, single bundle offer), it is not diverse — it is one concept being fatigued into the ground.

Set concept targets by spend band: sub-$100k/month, 1–3 concepts is fine; $100k–$500k/month, aim for around 2 winning concepts with 2–6 in testing; $500k+/month, aim for 3+ concepts and 4–5 core working funnels, unless you are targeting the US/worldwide where two scalable concepts can carry a lot of spend.
Sector-specific interpretation: in fashion, diverse concepts typically mean different products/categories; in CPG, typically different reframes of the same product.
If your concept coverage is far below the band for your spend, treat diversity as the creative bottleneck.
caveats: Concept-count targets are source heuristics, not verified benchmarks, and depend on market size and breadth.
Some format diversity is still needed (e.g., not running only statics); the point is to not over-index on format.

cards.title: Don't over-allocate to dynamic product ads
cards.summary: Keep DPAs as a small share of spend because they are bottom-of-funnel and rarely incremental.
cards.use_when: You are rebalancing spend inside a Meta account where DPAs are consuming the majority of budget.
steps: Check what percentage of account spend is in dynamic product ads.
If a large share (source flags accounts sitting near 70% of spend in DPAs), rebalance — DPAs are bottom of funnel and, in the source's view, not incremental.
Acknowledge DPAs can spend on cold and perform 'okay' there, but do not treat that as justification for the dominant share.
Move reallocated budget into diversified cold campaigns with concept-level creative.
caveats: '70%' and 'not incremental' are the source's observations/opinions, not measured facts across all accounts.
DPA performance varies by category and catalog size; validate with your own incrementality read.

cards.title: Analyze winners to replicate the source of success
cards.summary: When an ad wins, diagnose which variable caused the win and consciously replicate that variable.
cards.use_when: You have recently found a winning creative and are deciding whether to iterate on it or chase entirely new ideas.
steps: Do not abandon a winner to search for whatever comes next — the source says some accounts find a winner and never replicate on it.
Decompose the winner across variables: persona, angle, offer, format, script structure, influencer/talent, and any other material difference.
Identify which variable drove the result (the source asks explicitly: was it the persona, the angle, the format, the scripting, the influencer or the talent?).
Brief the creative team to produce variations that hold the winning variable constant and vary the rest, to validate and extend the win.
Feed this back into the creative roadmap so winners inform the next production cycle.
caveats: Attribution of a win to a single variable is inherently uncertain; treat it as a hypothesis to test in the next round.
Winners decay over time — this is about reinforcement, not indefinite reuse.

cards.title: Run creative production as a system with a feedback loop
cards.summary: Replace ad-hoc creative production with a continuous system that ingests performance feedback.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or reviewing your creative roadmap and production cadence against a scale target.
steps: Ask whether creative is shot reactively when ads are needed, or produced continuously against a roadmap.
If ad hoc, build a consistent production system that puts a high volume of assets into the account on an ongoing basis.
Include a feedback loop: performance data from live creative should feed back into the briefing and production process.
Set expected volume using the spend-based rule or a churn/average-winner model, and check whether production capacity genuinely matches it.
Align internal creative team skills or agency selection to the required volume and quality standard; the source notes this may require upskilling the team or changing creative agencies.
caveats: Source does not prescribe a specific production tool or headcount — the requirement is output against volume and quality targets.
Volume targets should be revisited as spend scales, per the diminishing-returns caveat.

cards.title: Drill down from business metrics to the ad that's the bottleneck
cards.summary: Trace a constraint top-down from business revenue to platform, campaign, adset, and ad to locate the actual driver.
cards.use_when: You have identified a top-level problem (e.g., rising CAC) and need to find where in the account it lives.
steps: Start at the top with business numbers: Shopify revenue, new customer revenue, and CAC.
Identify the level of the problem (e.g., CAC issue), then go into Meta and Google and determine which platform.
Within the failing platform, go into campaigns, then adsets, then ads, until you reach the element holding back performance.
Confirm the diagnosis with data-integrity checks (platform ROAS versus acquisition MER) before making structural decisions.
Sequence the fixes: generally data integrity first, then account structure, then creative — the source notes creative often has the highest impact but the longest fix time.
caveats: Order of fixes is a source heuristic, not a universal law; the appropriate sequence can vary with business context.
If your metrics are not trustworthy, do not attempt to diagnose deeper levels until the data-integrity layer is fixed.

cards.title: Fix data integrity before creative or account structure
cards.summary: If platform metrics do not correlate with business KPIs, treat that as the top-priority bottleneck before anything else.
cards.use_when: You are sequencing a paid-media turnaround and deciding what to fix first.
steps: Check whether a large gap exists between acquisition MER and platform-attributed ROAS.

If the gap is large and unresolved by attribution-setting changes, make data integrity the number-one bottleneck — the source's rationale is that you cannot do valid creative analysis or account structuring on metrics that are not causally tied to business outcomes.
Complete the data-integrity work first (attribution settings, breakdown-based reporting, fixed P&L and first-time P&L).
Then fix account structure, which the source describes as a relatively fast, high-leverage fix (consolidating campaigns, removing bleed into existing customers, fixing settings errors).
Then move into creative, which the source treats as high-impact but slow to fix because it requires structural changes to production capability.
caveats: This ordering is a source opinion based on their client portfolio, not an empirical sequence validated across all businesses.
Some businesses with accurate data may benefit from starting on creative instead.

If CAC rose while volume tripled or quadrupled, the trade-off can be worth it.","Use the trend to decide whether to scale, hold and optimize, or pull back — the source warns that forcing unprofitable cohorts puts you in a bad position 3–6 months later."],"caveats":["This GP-to-CAC figure is first-purchase only, so the source notes it is not technically lifetime gross profit.","No universal benchmark is established; the ratio bands are source heuristics."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","measurement","customer-acquisition-cost","gross-profit","cohort-analysis","unit-economics","trend-analysis"]},{"title":"GP-to-CAC ratio bands for scale, hold, or pull back","summary":"Use first-purchase gross profit divided by CAC to judge whether current economics justify scaling spend.","use_when":"You are deciding whether to increase ad budgets, hold flat, or cut spend based on first-order profitability.","steps":["Calculate the ratio as first-purchase gross profit in dollars divided by CAC for the current month and over time.","Interpret per the source's bands: under 1 means you lose money on the first purchase (high bankruptcy risk unless you are a well-capitalized CPG with strong retention); 1–2 is 'fine' but generally not scale-worthy without strong retention; 2–3 is the target zone where the source says scale; above 3 means you are likely leaving money on the table.","Adjust these bands for retention: strong repeat purchase behavior supports a higher CAC tolerance and a lower first-purchase ratio, and weak retention requires being very profitable on first purchase because people do not buy again.","Check the trend line, not just the current month: deteriorating ratio over the last 6 months is the signal to investigate before scaling."],"caveats":["Bands are source-specific heuristics, not calculated benchmarks.","The source notes these bands assume no other acquisition channel is excluded from the calculation.","Figure is first-purchase only, not true lifetime gross profit."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","measurement","customer-acquisition-cost","gross-profit","pricing","retention","scaling"]},{"title":"Normalized P&L for volume verification","summary":"Build a 2–2.5 year normalized P&L to check whether contribution margin improves or degrades as you ramp ad spend.","use_when":"You are verifying whether scaling ad spend produced profitable volume or just bought top-line revenue.","steps":["Structure the P&L: gross revenue minus refunds/returns minus discounts plus shipping collected equals net revenue; then subtract cost of goods sold, shipping and fulfillment, and transaction fees to reach gross margin; then subtract marketing (all channels in one line); this yields contribution profit/margin.","Enter monthly data for the last 2–2.5 years.","If you are an in-house brand, you may continue down through operating expenses to EBITDA; if you are an agency doing a client audit, stop before operating expenses — the source says they are not needed.","Track the contribution margin trend: if margin is falling while you are ramping ad spend, that scaling attempt failed.","Identify at what spend level the failure happened and what assumptions about generating more revenue at higher spend proved wrong.","Use this to confirm or contradict the unit-level CAC read from the cohort model."],"caveats":["Refunds, discounts, shipping collected, and fee structures vary by commerce system and accounting method.","The source describes this as a verification step, not the primary metric."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","measurement","p-and-l","contribution-margin","gross-profit","scaling","unit-economics"]},{"title":"First-time-customer P&L to expose weak acquisition","summary":"Filter out returning-customer revenue to see true new-customer acquisition performance and compute acquisition MER.","use_when":"Your blended P&L looks healthy but you suspect paid acquisition is actually underperforming.","steps":["Regenerate the P&L filtering out all returning-customer orders, keeping only first-time orders.","Compare it to the blended P&L: the source notes that accumulated repeat revenue can make an eight- or nine-figure retailer's acquisition look far better than it is.","Compute acquisition MER from this filtered P&L: new customer revenue divided by ad spend.","Use this acquisition MER as the reference point for the data-integrity comparison against platform ROAS.","The source's illustrative range: large retailers often see acquisition MER of roughly 3x to 7x — for every $1 of ad spend, $3–$7 of new customer revenue; a $100k monthly spend would mean $300k–$700k in new customer sales."],"caveats":["The 3x–7x figure is an illustrative example from the source, not a benchmark.","Filtering methods depend on how your commerce system tags first-time versus repeat orders."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","measurement","attribution","p-and-l","new-customer-acquisition","retention","roas"]},{"title":"Reconcile platform ROAS with acquisition MER","summary":"Detect over-attribution by comparing platform account-wide ROAS against the acquisition MER from your first-time P&L.","use_when":"You are deciding whether to trust Meta, Google, TikTok, or Pinterest reported ROAS for budget decisions.","steps":["Pull the account-wide ROAS from each platform and place it next to the acquisition MER from the first-time P&L.","If the gap is large (the source's example: P&L says $3–$7 back per dollar, Meta account-wide says 17), suspect one-day-view attribution crediting conversions to people who would have bought anyway, or overspend on existing customers inflating the number.","On Meta, click columns, run an attribution-setting breakdown, and inspect 7-day click and 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view, plus incremental attribution.","The source says in ~95% of accounts these tighter settings correlate much better with acquisition MER.","Choose one: switch all attribution settings to the tightest-correlating option, or keep current settings but judge performance using the breakdown numbers rather than the headline ROAS.","On TikTok and Pinterest, pull 7-day-click ROAS; the source says one-day view typically inflates TikTok substantially and 7-day click will drop toward (or below) acquisition MER. Repeat the correlation exercise for every platform."],"caveats":["The 17x versus 3–7x and the ~95% figure are source illustrations/assertions, not measured guarantees.","Attribution interface labels and available breakdowns change; verify the current platform UI before acting."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","attribution","measurement","roas","meta-ads","tiktok-ads","data-integrity"]},{"title":"Google: check brand/non-brand split and non-brand correlation","summary":"Keep brand and non-brand campaigns cleanly separated and test non-brand ROAS against acquisition MER.","use_when":"You are evaluating whether Google Search/Shopping is genuinely acquiring new customers or harvesting existing demand.","steps":["Do not tighten Google's wide default attribution windows — the source says Google is data-reliant and recommends leaving long windows in place rather than narrowing them.","Instead, check for clear separation between branded and non-branded campaigns; brand keywords appearing in non-brand campaigns (or vice versa) is an immediate red flag to fix.","Look at your non-branded campaigns' ROAS against acquisition MER. If they do not correlate, investigate three possibilities: (a) they are genuinely outperforming and you may be underspending on Google, (b) they are mislabeled — pulling brand or bottom-of-funnel traffic driven from other channels, or (c) there is a setup/attribution problem.","Only after ruling out (a) and (b) should you conclude it is a setup issue."],"caveats":["Google's attribution defaults and reports change; verify current settings in the interface.","Bottom-of-funnel and cross-channel halo effects make Google ROAS misreadings common in the source's experience."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","google-ads","attribution","measurement","search-terms","new-customer-acquisition","roas"]},{"title":"Isolate a test to resolve attribution ambiguity","summary":"When correlation between platform ROAS and business MER stays unresolved, run a controlled incrementality test instead of guessing.","use_when":"You cannot tell whether a platform (Meta, Google, TikTok) is genuinely driving incremental new-customer revenue.","steps":["Once you have compared platform ROAS to acquisition MER and attribution-setting changes still do not reconcile them, do not keep spending on an assumption — design a test.","For eight- and nine-figure brands, the source uses causal geo-lift experiments, typically run over about 25 days, to validate a platform's incrementality.","For brand-spend incrementality, use a clustering algorithm to pull brand spend from selected states and measure the effect, if the business believes brand is incremental.","Write clear parameters before launching so the result is readable; the output should either confirm performance or confirm a setup problem."],"caveats":["~25 days is the source's typical duration, not a fixed rule.","Geo tests require sufficient volume; the source frames this as an eight/nine-figure technique."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","experiment-design","measurement","incrementality","geo-test","attribution","budget-allocation"]},{"title":"Evaluate retention to set CAC targets","summary":"Benchmark gross-profit retention curves by day 90, 180, and 365 to decide how much first-purchase CAC you can tolerate.","use_when":"You are setting acquisition budget targets and need to know whether high first-order CAC is justified by repeat purchasing.","steps":["Build a cohort analysis at gross profit level over time.","Examine the percentage growth in gross profit at day 90, day 180, and day 365.","Compare your curve against portfolio averages for comparable brands/categories — the source contrasts e.g. fashion brands against each other.","Use the result to adjust CAC tolerance: strong retention means a higher acceptable CAC and lower first-purchase GP-to-CAC requirement; poor retention means first purchase must be highly profitable because people do not buy again.","Feed the adjusted tolerance back into your new-customer KPI targets."],"caveats":["Pulling these numbers is described as complicated; the source does not give universal growth benchmarks in this video.","Comparisons are to the source's client-portfolio averages, which are category-dependent."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","retention","measurement","cohort-analysis","customer-acquisition-cost","gross-profit","subscriptions"]},{"title":"One cold campaign until business complexity forces a split","summary":"Start account structure from a single cold campaign and require a defendable purpose for every additional campaign.","use_when":"You are restructuring a Meta or Google ad account or reviewing whether campaign count is inflated.","steps":["Ask: how many campaigns exist, and what is the defendable purpose of each one? Write each purpose into a spreadsheet column next to the campaign.","Error-check each campaign against its stated purpose (exclusions, settings, creative) as you go.","Cut any campaign you cannot defend with a clear commercial argument and consolidate; the source says this is common even in accounts spending $1M–$5M/month, and consolidation usually improves performance.","Do not add complexity for spend's sake — the source says complexity is required by business complexity, not budget size.","Legitimate causes of fragmentation include multiple countries/sub-brands/regions where you want to shift budget selectively (e.g., Australia vs New Zealand), or a fast-turning product portfolio where you need to pull budget on one category (e.g., dresses) and read results quickly.","If your agency cannot articulate why each campaign exists, treat that as a reason to consolidate."],"caveats":["This is the source's operating thesis for their managed accounts, not an industry rule.","Meta 'campaign count' heuristics change with platform behavior; validate against current performance."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","ad-account-structure","meta-ads","budget-allocation","consolidation","campaign-architecture"]},{"title":"Check frequency across new, engaged, and existing audiences","summary":"Use 30-day frequency on new/engaged/existing segments to find overspend and weak top-of-funnel content.","use_when":"You are diagnosing audience-segment budget distribution or diagnosing creative fatigue in your Meta account.","steps":["Split budget analysis by three segments: new, engaged, and existing — the source says look at frequency, not percentage split, across these.","If 30-day frequency on existing is extreme (source example: 30), you are overspending on existing customers and should cut that spend.","If frequency on engaged is high (source example: 14), you have too much middle-of-funnel creative and should reduce it in favor of more top-of-funnel assets.","Treat high engaged frequency as a symptom of content that is not top-of-funnel enough, or of existing-customer spend bleeding into all campaigns instead of being controlled in a dedicated campaign.","Fix by launching more genuinely top-of-funnel assets and containing existing-customer spend to one dedicated campaign."],"caveats":["The 30 and 14 figures are illustrative source examples, not universal thresholds.","Ideal frequency varies by category and offer; do not treat a single frequency number as a target without context."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","audience-segmentation","frequency","meta-ads","creative-strategy","budget-allocation","existing-customers"]},{"title":"Standardize on 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view","summary":"Adopt a single tight attribution setting across the account and keep it consistent.","use_when":"You are configuring Meta attribution settings or auditing whether settings are inconsistent across campaigns.","steps":["Check whether attribution settings are consistent across all campaigns; inconsistency changes reported ROAS between campaigns and muddies comparisons.","Choose a tighter setting that correlates better with your P&L; the source's go-to is 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view.","Note the source's explanation for including engaged views: Meta changed the definition roughly three months before the video so that likes/comments/shares and 5-second views are no longer counted in 7-day click, so 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view is roughly equivalent to the previously preferred 7-day click.","Apply the same attribution setting everywhere, then use attribution-setting breakdowns when judging performance (see reconcile-platform-roas card)."],"caveats":["The specific definition change and closure equivalence is time-sensitive; verify current Meta documentation.","A 'tighter' setting is a business-fit choice, not universally optimal — the source notes it correlates better with their P&L."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","attribution","meta-ads","measurement","reporting","data-integrity"]},{"title":"Audit campaign naming against actual settings and creative","summary":"Confirm that campaign/adset naming matches the targeting, objective, and creative actually running underneath.","use_when":"You are doing a housekeeping pass or suspect high-ROAS 'cold' campaigns are mislabeled warm or existing-customer campaigns.","steps":["For each campaign/adset, compare the name to the actual audience definition, placement, objective, and the ads beneath it.","Flag mismatches: source notes a campaign labeled 'cold top of funnel' frequently turns out to target existing customers and serve bottom-of-funnel assets, making its ROAS look great when it is not actually acquiring cold customers.","If names use awareness stages (e.g., 'problem aware'), verify the ads actually match that stage (a 'problem aware' adset running a bunch of solution-aware ads is a defect even if the name looks competent).","Treat naming mismatch as a diagnosis gap: the account is claiming something the traffic and creative are not delivering."],"caveats":["Naming conventions vary; the criterion is whether the label accurately describes the audience and creative, not a specific label format."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","ad-account-structure","measurement","diagnosis","meta-ads","creative-strategy"]},{"title":"Common Meta settings errors worth fixing","summary":"A short list of concrete Meta account errors: undefined segments, App Rewards placements, legacy lookalike/interest targeting on purchase objectives, missing existing-customer exclusions.","use_when":"You are doing a settings-and-targeting error sweep on a Meta account during a structure audit.","steps":["Set definitions on new, engaged, and existing audiences rather than leaving them undefined.","Kill App Rewards placements — the source says they have never seen an App Rewards placement drive a single purchase, and local/store-driving engaged-view campaigns bleed into this placement.","Do not use legacy targeting methods (lookalikes, interest targeting) on purchase objectives for ecommerce; the source would not use them for 99% of accounts, reserving them for specific non-purchase cases.","Verify existing customers are actually excluded from cold campaigns.","Confirm naming matches settings and creative (see separate card)."],"caveats":["'99% of accounts' and the no-purchases-from-App-Rewards claim are the source's stated opinions/experience, not measured benchmarks.","Placement options and defaults change over time; verify in the current ads manager."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","meta-ads","targeting","placements","exclusions","ad-account-structure","audit"]},{"title":"Google-specific audit checks: search terms, feed, currency","summary":"Audit Google by checking brand leakage in cold campaigns, Merchant Center feed completeness, and multi-currency feed setup.","use_when":"You are auditing Google Ads and Google Merchant Center ahead of a seasonal peak or a restructure.","steps":["Open each cold campaign, go to search terms, and verify branded terms are not pulling through into cold campaigns.","Check the Google Merchant Center feed: optimize titles, fill in all relevant feed variables, and eliminate warnings and errors.","If selling across multiple countries, use a multi-currency feed — the source warns that running everything through a single currency triggers auto-conversion and adds tax as it presents in Shopping, hurting performance.","Then investigate the halo effect: Google often sits bottom-of-funnel, so check whether cold search-term demand is genuinely converting cold traffic.","If ROAS on non-brand campaigns does not correlate with acquisition MER after these checks, the source usually proposes an incrementality test for Google — but only when they suspect a halo effect or need rigorous validation."],"caveats":["The source notes Google can be a strong new-customer channel — one of their own brands was Google-only and reached a seven-figure run rate around 2019–2020 — so Google is not inherently bottom-of-funnel.","Feed and interface details change; verify current GMC and Google Ads UI."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","google-ads","merchant-center","shopping","search-terms","feed-optimization","incrementality"]},{"title":"Creative volume rule: one new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend","summary":"Size your creative production requirement by anchoring new ads per month to monthly ad spend.","use_when":"You are deciding whether creative volume is the bottleneck or setting a production target for your creative team or agency.","steps":["Divide monthly ad spend by $1,000 to get a baseline monthly new-ad target (source example: $100k/month implies ~100 new ads per month).","Treat this as a rough rule of thumb, not a linear law — the source says at $1–3M/month you likely do not need 3,000 assets, and there are diminishing returns to raw creative volume at large scale.","If you need a more precise target, use one of two models: (a) a churn model — monthly churn rate of winners implies a replacement rate; combine with hit rate to back into volume; or (b) average winner spend and revenue generation — if an average winner generates $20k, use that and your win rate to back-propagate to volume.","If your actual output is far below the rule-of-thumb target, treat creative volume as a likely bottleneck."],"caveats":["$1,000/ad is explicitly a simplification; the source's real models are described as complicated.","Churn-model inputs (winner churn, hit rate, average winner revenue) are business-specific and must come from your own account."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","creative-strategy","creative-velocity","production-planning","budget-allocation","scaling"]},{"title":"Separate volume, diversity, and quality as the creative bottleneck","summary":"Creative bottlenecks are one of exactly three: insufficient volume, insufficient concept diversity, or insufficient quality.","use_when":"You are diagnosing why creative performance has plateaued and need to pick the right fix.","steps":["First check volume against your spend-based target (see the $1,000/new-ad card); if output is far off, that is the bottleneck.","If volume is fine, check diversity — specifically concept diversification, not format diversification (see concept-diversity card).","If both volume and diversity are adequate, assess quality by reading the actual scripts and content, judging angles, personas, scripting, talent, and offer. This is the hardest to systematize and requires direct-response marketing judgment; the source recommends looking at the ads directly and rescripting/reshooting what is weak.","Assign exactly one bottleneck at a time — the source emphasizes you only have one creative bottleneck at any moment; pick it and fix it before moving on."],"caveats":["Quality has no SOP in the source — it requires domain judgment and reviewing actual creative.","You may end up with a different bottleneck than the source would call it if your spend model differs."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","creative-strategy","diagnosis","creative-velocity","ad-copywriting","quality-control"]},{"title":"Diversify concepts, not just formats","summary":"Measure creative diversity by angle/offer/persona concept coverage rather than by mix of UGC, statics, and other formats.","use_when":"You are planning creative strategy for a scaling account or diagnosing why a single winning ad fatigues.","steps":["Define concepts as a combination of angle, offer, and persona — not format (video vs static vs UGC). The source says people over-index on format diversity and under-index on concept diversity.","Illustration: a creatine brand spending $200k/month may be launching 200 ads/month but if all spend sits behind one concept (e.g., men 25–45, gym-performance angle, single bundle offer), it is not diverse — it is one concept being fatigued into the ground.","Set concept targets by spend band: sub-$100k/month, 1–3 concepts is fine; $100k–$500k/month, aim for around 2 winning concepts with 2–6 in testing; $500k+/month, aim for 3+ concepts and 4–5 core working funnels, unless you are targeting the US/worldwide where two scalable concepts can carry a lot of spend.","Sector-specific interpretation: in fashion, diverse concepts typically mean different products/categories; in CPG, typically different reframes of the same product.","If your concept coverage is far below the band for your spend, treat diversity as the creative bottleneck."],"caveats":["Concept-count targets are source heuristics, not verified benchmarks, and depend on market size and breadth.","Some format diversity is still needed (e.g., not running only statics); the point is to not over-index on format."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","creative-strategy","concept-diversification","ad-creative","scaling","fatigue-management","brand-vs-cpg"]},{"title":"Don't over-allocate to dynamic product ads","summary":"Keep DPAs as a small share of spend because they are bottom-of-funnel and rarely incremental.","use_when":"You are rebalancing spend inside a Meta account where DPAs are consuming the majority of budget.","steps":["Check what percentage of account spend is in dynamic product ads.","If a large share (source flags accounts sitting near 70% of spend in DPAs), rebalance — DPAs are bottom of funnel and, in the source's view, not incremental.","Acknowledge DPAs can spend on cold and perform 'okay' there, but do not treat that as justification for the dominant share.","Move reallocated budget into diversified cold campaigns with concept-level creative."],"caveats":["'70%' and 'not incremental' are the source's observations/opinions, not measured facts across all accounts.","DPA performance varies by category and catalog size; validate with your own incrementality read."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","meta-ads","retargeting","budget-allocation","creative-strategy","incrementality","dynamic-product-ads"]},{"title":"Analyze winners to replicate the source of success","summary":"When an ad wins, diagnose which variable caused the win and consciously replicate that variable.","use_when":"You have recently found a winning creative and are deciding whether to iterate on it or chase entirely new ideas.","steps":["Do not abandon a winner to search for whatever comes next — the source says some accounts find a winner and never replicate on it.","Decompose the winner across variables: persona, angle, offer, format, script structure, influencer/talent, and any other material difference.","Identify which variable drove the result (the source asks explicitly: was it the persona, the angle, the format, the scripting, the influencer or the talent?).","Brief the creative team to produce variations that hold the winning variable constant and vary the rest, to validate and extend the win.","Feed this back into the creative roadmap so winners inform the next production cycle."],"caveats":["Attribution of a win to a single variable is inherently uncertain; treat it as a hypothesis to test in the next round.","Winners decay over time — this is about reinforcement, not indefinite reuse."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","creative-strategy","iteration","ad-testing","ad-copywriting","talent-selection","roadmap"]},{"title":"Run creative production as a system with a feedback loop","summary":"Replace ad-hoc creative production with a continuous system that ingests performance feedback.","use_when":"You are setting up or reviewing your creative roadmap and production cadence against a scale target.","steps":["Ask whether creative is shot reactively when ads are needed, or produced continuously against a roadmap.","If ad hoc, build a consistent production system that puts a high volume of assets into the account on an ongoing basis.","Include a feedback loop: performance data from live creative should feed back into the briefing and production process.","Set expected volume using the spend-based rule or a churn/average-winner model, and check whether production capacity genuinely matches it.","Align internal creative team skills or agency selection to the required volume and quality standard; the source notes this may require upskilling the team or changing creative agencies."],"caveats":["Source does not prescribe a specific production tool or headcount — the requirement is output against volume and quality targets.","Volume targets should be revisited as spend scales, per the diminishing-returns caveat."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","creative-strategy","production-planning","creative-velocity","roadmap","agency-management","systems"]},{"title":"Drill down from business metrics to the ad that's the bottleneck","summary":"Trace a constraint top-down from business revenue to platform, campaign, adset, and ad to locate the actual driver.","use_when":"You have identified a top-level problem (e.g., rising CAC) and need to find where in the account it lives.","steps":["Start at the top with business numbers: Shopify revenue, new customer revenue, and CAC.","Identify the level of the problem (e.g., CAC issue), then go into Meta and Google and determine which platform.","Within the failing platform, go into campaigns, then adsets, then ads, until you reach the element holding back performance.","Confirm the diagnosis with data-integrity checks (platform ROAS versus acquisition MER) before making structural decisions.","Sequence the fixes: generally data integrity first, then account structure, then creative — the source notes creative often has the highest impact but the longest fix time."],"caveats":["Order of fixes is a source heuristic, not a universal law; the appropriate sequence can vary with business context.","If your metrics are not trustworthy, do not attempt to diagnose deeper levels until the data-integrity layer is fixed."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","diagnosis","measurement","ad-account-structure","creative-strategy","prioritization","root-cause-analysis"]},{"title":"Fix data integrity before creative or account structure","summary":"If platform metrics do not correlate with business KPIs, treat that as the top-priority bottleneck before anything else.","use_when":"You are sequencing a paid-media turnaround and deciding what to fix first.","steps":["Check whether a large gap exists between acquisition MER and platform-attributed ROAS.","If the gap is large and unresolved by attribution-setting changes, make data integrity the number-one bottleneck — the source's rationale is that you cannot do valid creative analysis or account structuring on metrics that are not causally tied to business outcomes.","Complete the data-integrity work first (attribution settings, breakdown-based reporting, fixed P&L and first-time P&L).","Then fix account structure, which the source describes as a relatively fast, high-leverage fix (consolidating campaigns, removing bleed into existing customers, fixing settings errors).","Then move into creative, which the source treats as high-impact but slow to fix because it requires structural changes to production capability."],"caveats":["This ordering is a source opinion based on their client portfolio, not an empirical sequence validated across all businesses.","Some businesses with accurate data may benefit from starting on creative instead."],"tags":["ad-copy-deployment","prioritization","measurement","data-integrity","ad-account-structure","creative-strategy","turnaround"]}]}

The argument that Conversion Rate is a vanity metric and should be replaced by Revenue Per Visitor (RPV), which belongs in 06-MEA.

Scope mix. Mostly growth, because testing discipline is gated on volume.

Volume. 15 to 20.

In this video, I'll be running you through exactly how we audit eight and nine figure ad accounts. I'll be running you through exactly the step-by-step process that we use to put together our audits that we give away for free to eight and nine figure brands so that you can do this process yourself on your own account. For context, we have over $400 million a year in ad spend under management. We actively work with 60 eight and nine figure brands and we have collectively as an agency over the course of the last six years completed at least a thousand audits across 6 7 8 9 and 10 figure businesses. So we have a lot of context when it comes down to the common mistakes that businesses make and also the common mistakes that agencies make when they go and put an audit together. So what a normal audit will look like from a regular agency is it will just be a list of settings errors. It'll be a PDF or a word document and it will just have 40 plus screenshots in it talking about trends and generic recommendations as to what you should do. Now, this is not a useful audit at all. Settings errors can sometimes be helpful, but a lot of the time they're just subjective. It's one agency saying this bidding strategy is better than another one, and it's not actually contextualized to the business. And not only that, it often doesn't matter. This is a 1enter at best. Now, what does actually matter? What should an audit be? and what are you going to learn over the course of this video? An audit should be a diagnosis of the constraint within the business. So identifying what is the bottleneck, what is the constraint, diagnosing it, and then providing clear next steps. There's likely multiple things to focus on. So if there are multiple recommendations provided, they're ordered carefully by commercial impact. And this prioritization becomes a road map in a way where you know exactly what the number one bottleneck is, then what's going to arise next. So you know how to work through the audit systematically over a 90-day period. And then we will always deliver audits. Now you're doing this for yourself, but this is just context. We will always deliver them in the form of a Loom video that walks you through in the accounts in the business in the models that we put together a very clear outlook as to here is actually what's going wrong. You can see it visually on the screen. Here is where we're looking and then here is exactly how you solve it. And we can walk you through that visually, too. It ends up being a very digestible way to understand what the diagnosis of the constraint and what the commercial impact is and priorities in a in a format that can very easily be distributed throughout the team as well compared to just a massive document with a bunch of screenshots with a lack of prioritization and it's just a bunch of generic stuff thrown in. So the very first thing is how to structure an audit. Now we will structure our audits. In fact, this is on our website. It's all over the place in our content through what we see as the three core pillars or the three schools of thought that exist within paid media in the context of e-commerce. Number one is technical account structure. This is the way that you're currently setting up and structuring the meta and Google ad accounts as well as the testing methodology for introducing new tests, new experiments over time. Number two is creative. More specifically, it's creative velocity, which is the rate in which you're introducing new creative into the account and the diversity set of those ads. Number three is data integrity and assurance. So, this is assuring that the metrics that you use within the platforms is actually steping up correlated with the actual business's KPIs. And so we're making sure that if you're looking at a rorowaz number to optimize, does that rorowaz number actually have a causal relationship to acquisition me in the business? So whatever the core metric is that we're measuring in the business, or are we making decisions on metrics that are flawed? So we really want to make sure there's data integrity here. Now, this will change dramatically based on the size that you're at. This portion of the audit looks very different if you're doing seven figures versus eight figures versus 9 versus if you have retail versus if you have a wholesale arm. All of these things start to come into play. Same for technical account structure. This materially changes as you step stone up into different revenue brackets, spend brackets and different industries. And the same thing applies less. So, this is more generic, but it still does translate into creative, which is that your creative is going to look materially different in a fashion brand compared to a CPG brand.
